did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezekiel quotes a popular proverb: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge”—meaning that children suffer because of their fathers’ sins. The chapter rejects this idea.
Did you know? The chapter states that all people belong to the Lord, and therefore establishes this principle: “The soul who sins shall die”—each person is responsible for their own actions.
Did you know? Ezekiel describes a righteous person not merely as someone who believes, but also as someone who practices “justice and righteousness” and treats others honestly.

Did you know? Among the righteous acts listed in the chapter are returning a pledge, refraining from robbery, giving bread to the hungry, and covering the naked with clothing—examples of social and moral responsibility.

Did you know? After describing the righteous person’s deeds, the chapter declares: “He is righteous; he shall surely live”—keeping the Lord’s laws and doing what is right are presented as the way of life.
Did you know? A wicked son is not declared righteous because of his father’s righteousness: if he himself commits the acts described in the chapter, he is judged according to his own actions.

Did you know? Ezekiel explicitly states the principle of personal responsibility: a son does not bear the guilt of his father, nor does a father bear the guilt of his son; each person’s righteousness or wickedness is attributed to that person.

Did you know? According to the chapter, when a wicked person turns away from all their sins, keeps the Lord’s laws, and practices justice and righteousness, their former sins are not remembered, and they will live.
Did you know? Even a past marked by righteousness does not exempt someone who turns away from that path and does wrong; the chapter emphasizes that judgment is based on the path a person follows.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the Lord calls Israel to turn back from their transgressions, cast them away, make for themselves “a new heart and a new spirit,” and choose life, because he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death.
